Knysna: The aftermath

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
This story is about the reality in Knysna now, now that the adrenaline of
the horror has passed, and 100’s of residents are faced with an
uncertain future. We look at various issues – we start off by reminding
viewers of the total chaos – and we tell the story of the evacuation
from the beaches at Belvedere, by small craft. We describe how many
people are suffering from stress and we hear from a therapist how
people are struggling emotionally to deal with their losses. We hear
from three people who have lost everything. Apart from donations, and
the incredible work done by volunteers, their futures remain very
bleak. Especially since 60 per cent did not have insurance. The money
coming from the WC Govt is mainly for infrastructure rebuilding and
going for the poor. We also hear how some residents are so fed up with
insurance companies that a Facebook has been started to name and
shame insurance companies. A disaster like this brings out the best in
people, and sometimes the worst – rental prices are going up
dramatically and developers are contacting people with no insurance,
wanting to buy up their properties. An ominous ending – Knysna is still
not out of the woods – roots are still burning in the indigenous forests,
and if heavy rain does not come and the wind starts blowing
dramatically, the fires could spring up again.

Press Release:


Rebuilding Knysna
Almost 2 months after the devastating Knysna fires damaged and destroyed properties and businesses, residents
have begun to rebuild their shattered lives. Despite the compassion of others however, many are struggling to
escape the trauma. Carte Blanche revisits a community still coming to terms with their losses

Script:


It was the worst fire to hit a town in south Africa since the 1860’s. Knysna became virtually encircled in flames.

LINK: As the flames closed in there was a rising sense of panic amongst the people living in Knysna as the escape routes were slowly but surely cut off. In fact, here in Belvedere the only option was a water evacuation.


The NSRI and commercial operators launched their craft into a hostile lagoon. Heading up operations was Jerome Simonis.

Jerome: The biggest problem was visibly. With 15 meters its very difficult to navigate on the lagoon here. We don’t practice for this type of evacuation where you've got wheel chairs involved, where you've got elderly frail people, where you've got animals involved. This was a one of a kind.


Media reports are emerging that one fire which started in the Elandskraal area was a result of a lightening strike. Footage allegedly taken 11 days before the June 7th inferno show a smoldering fire in the indigenous forest which was allegedly reported to fire authorities but not acted upon. The Knysna municipality say they can’t comment till their investigation is completed.

Still, roots are smoldering at Elandskraal - they are called peat fires, they spread slowly down the roots for several meters.

Wayne: Some of it is not under the ground, ins actually in what we call a peat, peat moss from years of the leaves and debris falling off the trees so its basically under that and there is a little air pocket and that’s where the fire gets its oxygen from.

50 millimeters of rainfall in this area is required to stop the slow burn.

Wayne: so we are monitoring it and if it does what we say come out of the bush towards an accessible area we will definitely take it on but its too risky to send the crews and the terrain isn’t accessible to vehicles or anything to be able to extinguish those smoldering fires

What ever the cause of the fire, it left a trial of utter destruction. and despair. Knysna resident Noma-Efese Pango still struggles to return to where her home once stood.

Noma: It was very stressful for me to come. I don’t like to come and see this because it stresses me so much.

LINK: Seven deaths, seven hundred homes completely destroyed and several hundred more damaged by the fire. IT's almost two months later and still people of knysna are battling to come to terms with this tragedy.


Compounding the misery is that over 50 per cent of residents were not insured like internationally acclaimed leather designer and manufacturer Aldo and Celia Kleyn. They did have household content insurance. Their workshop and stock valued around 2 million rand was wiped out.

Aldo: The main thing for me really is losing all my tools, my machinery, my sewing machines, things that we have gathered through the years that we have collected from various countries all over the world.

Interview

Also without insurance was Zak Liepner…. who lost his home and vehicles?

John: Did you ever imagine that you would be at this point in your life, being where you are? Surviving on the compassion of other people?

Zak: Yah, honestly I don’t wish this upon anyone, you know?

For those who had insurance, many have become frustrated. Business owner Evelin Pepler started a Facebook called after burn, for residents to share their experiences with their insurance companies.

JOHN: What sort of common complaints are you hearing?
EVELYN: Well the frustrations of settlement offer. Initial discussions around that are half of what they are insured for and massive deductions for things like paving that is left and retaining walls and a swimming pool. Despite the house being completely lost
John: So once you get a good idea of who the good guys are, who the bad guys are you might possibly expose the bad guys?
Evelyn: Yah, Yah I think we should.

One resident estate agent Lizette monk was so fed up by her insurance companies’ tardiness that she posted her story on social media.

Lizette: That was 2 o' clock the Thursday afternoon and by 4 o clock that same day I had signed off and they processing my payment.

John: And is there any doubt in your mind that going on social media is what clinched the deal for you.
Lizette: Absolutely.

The western cape govt has earmarked tens of millions of rand to the Knysna municipality, to help with the rebuild. Much of that money will be spend on infrastructure. But what about residents that have lost their homes.? Knysna Mayor Eleanor Bouw -spies says that those who are not insured do quality for help.

Mayor: That form of help we cannot change as we go along. ITs at the same standard form of help. So a person for instance within the area of white location qualifies for a home of 110 000 breaking new ground on. That goes to any other person who has not been insured.

Like for example in the more affluent areas. The council is wanting to be able to offer a cash equivalent of R110 000 for building materials as a kick start.

Big business, relief organizations and individuals continue to give generously and volunteers are working around the clock. Many home and business owners have provided accommodation for those displaced like Raja Mkwaila and his family who lost everything.

Raja: We feel bad. IT's painful to lose everything like that. It's very painful.

A local vet service where Raja works service has provided him and his family with a small office to live in.

LINK: Tragedies like this one often bring out the very best in people, sadly though, that’s no always the case.

Some call it supplies and demand, others profiteering…. many people we spoke to are desperate for alternative accommodation speak of increase rentals and this was conformed by estate agent Lizette Monk,

Lizette: The landlords are thinking that the insurance companies are paying astronomical amounts for rentals so across the board prices are going up I had a call yesterday where the lady was getting 5000 but an estate agent told her no but the one next door, she is now getting 8,5000 for the same thing. a two bedroom, two bathrooms. So I said well in that instance its purely greed due to the situation we are in with the fires.

LINK: IT; s only when you drive around Knysna that you begin to appreciate the extent of the devastation caused by the wild fires but then again how could you ever fully understand the extraordinary trauma suffered by this town and its people.

Norma-Efese lived here with her family for 20 years.

Noma-efese: It was our pride and everything to us because we do it with our own hands.

It’s the loss of irreplaceable sentimental belongings that often hurts the most.

John: Does it make you angry? Sorrowful?
Heinz: Frustrated. frustrated you know? Maybe it will come later. you know one always says men don’t cry you know.

Recognizing the community’s pain, psychologist Joanne Kaschula has started weekly trauma workshops for women

Joanne: There is a lot of grief. There is so much sadness. The loss is absolutely overwhelming and three are recurring themes that are coming up. Loss of material possessions for some you would say no its not that important but our things do define us. They are what we have collected over the years and they are part of our stories

Joanne plans to also hold men’s meetings. Sometimes it gets too much for Zack Liepner whose parents home too was destroyed.

Zac: Nah I think the only thing we can do is be positive. We've had so much help and love from everyone and you know, its hard, seeing my parents and stuff. That’s the hardest. Cause I’m worried about them you know. I am young. I can pull through this but...
JOHN: Are they okay how are they doing
Zac: Yah I would just hate something to happen to them. that’s all.

The knysna fire has re-traumatized the Kleyns. They told us they were in New York during 9/11 and lost everything. They decided to make a fresh start in Knysna.

Cilia: For me since from the tragedy at 9/11 which me and my husband are the survivors from that tragic event. We are now facing this fire, devastating fire that kills everything include our way of making a living.

Roughly 2500 residents lost their jobs and means of living.
Noma-efese: Yes, its very very difficult but I don’t know what we are going to do, because my husband is not working and I am just working three days a week, sometimes 2 days a week.
It’s a tough road ahead for the people of knysna who are buckling down to rebuild.

Aldo: Its a very traumatic experience and its very difficult to actually out it in words but we are survivors.
